newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew has little to celebrate on Space Day.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew has little to celebrate on Space Day.

text.p: Russia marks 36 years since it put the first man in space on Saturday, but a U.S.-Russian crew now in orbit aboard the Mir space station have little to celebrate.

NASA astronaut Jerry Linenger painted a disturbing picture of life on Moscow's 11-year-old Mir space station on Friday, just as Russian officials said the Mir crew might have a rare tipple to toast Space Day.

Speaking from space, Linenger said he and his two Russian colleagues had almost abandoned ship twice in the past few months and were making repairs to Mir's troubled cooling system in masks to avoid taking in toxic fumes from leaking coolant.
Temperatures and humidity aboard the station had soared when the cooling system failed and the crew were being forced to take parts from another device to fix Mir's main oxygen generators.
Despite the difficulties, an official at Russian space mission control said the crew might take time out to raise a toast to Space Day on Saturday.
But it would be a small one -- conditions in space mean that one large slug of cognac can render a cosmonaut totally drunk.
Moscow's first manned space mission in 1961 was the crowning glory of its space programme, driven for decades by fierce Cold War-era competition with Washington.
Long before relations began to thaw, the former Soviet Union was struggling to catch up with the United States.

A new report by Jane's defence analysis group said on Friday that Moscow had been trying to develop its own satellite defence network in the 1980s at the same time as attacking U.S. plans to build a "Star Wars" system.
Nowadays, the former foes cooperate, but Russia's financial struggles mean tensions still bubble beneath the surface.
NASA officials said recently they would review safety aboard Mir -- the world's only space station -- before sending any more astronauts to live there.

"It gets very complex very quickly," said Linenger. "We need to fix our problems," added the U.S. astronaut, who has been aboard Mir since January and is due to stay until next month, when the U.S. space shuttle Atlantis will pick him up.

Russian President Boris Yeltsin told the head of the Russian Space Agency on Friday that the space programme "had fallen back from its achievements" in the five years since the Soviet Union's collapse in 1991 and urged him to press for more funds.
"Have you got a direct line to me?" Yeltsin asked Yuri Koptev. "Put one in," he said, gesturing to a waiting official.

Koptev said after the meeting that the government had promised money to allow him to fund part of Russia's contribution to the $37 billion Alpha International Space Station which is due to replace Mir by 2003.
Western officials had threatened to drop Russia from the project after it reneged on its commitments in February.
On Mir, Linenger said repair gear brought by an unmanned Progress resupply ship on Tuesday had enabled them to mend one leak in the cooling systemn but there was another.
"We need to look closely at the result of the repairs and make sure we have a good environment for those that follow," he added, echoing the concerns expressed by NASA officials.
British-born astronaut Michael Foale is due to replace Linenger and two more Americans are also in line. Koptev said Russia earned $471 million hosting westerners on Mir last year.

Linenger said the crew had almost abandoned ship when a fire broke out on February 23 and later when they feared an out-of-control unmanned resupply ship could collide with the station. "It will always be nice to see Atlantis," he said.
